title: Roll puff pastry into an even 3 mm sheet with a spacer-ring rolling pin
instruction: Roll this puff pastry out into a 3 mm sheet at least 20 cm long.
context: Rolling dough out with a rolling pin, for a pie crust, cookies or pastry, is something most people have done at home, and spacer rings that slip onto a rolling pin are a common home tool for rolling it to an even thickness. The rings set the thickness only while both of them ride on the board, so the pin has to be kept level along its length: with one end lifted it leaves a wedge, thick on that side. Dough springs back, so it takes several passes to come down to the rings. Uneven puff pastry can bake unevenly, raw where thick and burnt where thin, and a sheet too short does not line the pan.
setup: Positions are in cm from the midpoint between the two arm bases, with x forward, y to the robot's left and the table top at z 0. Full scale. An oiled maple pastry board (mid brown, darker than the table) 31 cm deep (x) by 28 cm across (y) and 1.5 cm thick lies fixed on the table, spanning x 14 to 45 and y -14 to 14, top at z 1.5, lightly floured (a wooden pin slides on it with friction 0.15 static, 0.10 dynamic). On it lies a chilled block of puff pastry 6.5 cm (x) by 20 cm (y) by 1.0 cm thick (130 mL, about 130 g), centered at x 29.5, y 0 (the board's center). Behind the pastry, a wooden rolling pin lies in its rest with its axis along y at x 41.5, z 5: 43 cm overall and 450 g, a barrel 5 cm across and 26 cm long (y -13 to 13), a blue silicone spacer ring 5.6 cm across (3 mm proud of the barrel) and 1.5 cm wide on each end of the barrel (|y| 11.5 to 13), and dark wooden handles 2.5 cm across and 8.5 cm long (|y| 13 to 21.5). The rest is two fixed dark wooden cradles on the table just outside the board's sides, one under the outer end of each handle (|y| 19.5 to 21.5, 4.5 cm deep in x, centered at x 41.5), each a block whose top carries the handle at z 3.75 with a 5 mm lip 1 cm tall in front of and behind the handle; in it the rings are 7 mm above the board. The pastry is modeled: it has no collider, and is shown as 1 cm slabs as thick as the pastry there, colored by thickness (cream over 6.5 mm, golds down to golden at 2.5 to 3.5 mm on spec, tan and dark brown below 2.5 mm, which the model never reaches because the rings hold the barrel 3 mm up).
scoring: The sheet is read at the end, held 1 s, as 20 strips 1 cm wide along x. It is long enough when every strip is at least 20 cm long, the floor of a 20 cm square pan. It is on spec when at least 90 % of it is 3 mm thick within 0.5 mm: the rings' gap plus the springback a baker accepts; 10 % allows for trimmed ends. It is even when the strips' average thicknesses are within 0.5 mm of each other, since a pin with one end lifted leaves a wedge that can bake lopsided. The pin is put away when it is set down level within 3 degrees, in its rest or on its rings on the board (within 5 mm), and let go (a release check: no gripper touching it), because a held or tilted pin can still roll onto the sheet. The trial scores 1.0 when the sheet is long enough, on spec and even, and the pin is put away. It scores 0.5 when every strip is at least 18 cm long but the sheet is not finished (about one pass left), or when the sheet is finished but the pin is not put away. It scores 0.25 when every strip is at least 16 cm long and the sheet is even, about two level passes. Otherwise it scores 0, including when the robot does nothing, makes one pass, or leaves a wedge. Possible scores: 0, 0.25, 0.5, 1.0. Where the arms end is not scored. In the simulation only, the model presses the pastry while both grippers touch the pin. This is an approximation, because the sim's pin slides on its rings instead of turning and cannot tell rolling from pushing; a stroke with fewer hands presses nothing but is not penalized. The real trial has no hand rule: it scores only the measured sheet and the final pin state, so a sheet rolled partly or wholly with one hand scores like any other. Real trial: lay a 1 cm grid transparency on the sheet, lined up with the board's front edge and center line, and measure the length along both edges and the middle with a ruler. Read thickness with a digital tire tread depth gauge (zeroed on the board, foot resting on the pastry, pin pushed through) at fixed points: the center of each 2 cm grid square the pastry covers (about 100 points), and every 2 cm along lines 0.5 cm in from each end and side. On spec is the share of points at 2.5 to 3.5 mm. Even means the 2 cm bands running the sheet's length average within 0.5 mm of each other. A point under 2.5 mm, a hole or a tear counts as off spec, since a ringed pin cannot press below 3 mm. Check the pin with a level app and a ruler, and the last frames for a finger on it.
reset_notes: The pastry is consumed: each real trial needs a fresh block of chilled store-bought puff pastry, cut and pressed into 6.5 x 20 x 1 cm (130 g), set centered at x 29.5, y 0, 20 to 30 minutes out of the fridge (about 18 C, 64 F). Scrape the board clean and re-flour it, put the pin back in its rest (axis along y), check both rings are on the barrel ends.
fidelity: The pastry is a model (doughkit) with no collider: the pin rides on its rings, and each slice the barrel crosses is pressed to the gap plus half its excess (springback, an estimate), volume kept. It presses only while both hands touch the pin, a stand-in for rolling since the pin slides rather than turns; the real trial has no hand rule. The dough gives no rolling resistance, so the rings keep the pin level however it is held. It cannot tear or go below 3 mm; a depth gauge checks a real sheet.
